newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Brazzaville quiet as truce deadline passes.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville quiet as truce deadline passes.

text.p: The Congo Republic's capital Brazzaville was calm on Tuesday after the start of yet another truce intended to end political and ethnic violence that has killed hundreds.

Witnesses said the guns fell silent after a flurry of shelling less than two hours before the midnight Monday (2300 GMT) deadline for the truce, initialled by President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor Denis Sassou Nguesso on Saturday.

Sources close to mediation efforts said Gabon's veteran President Omar Bongo planned to send a plane to the battered city on Tuesday to take representatives of the warring parties to peace talks in his capital Libreville.
"In principle the military should have given instructions for a ceasefire to come into force," one source close to mediation efforts told Reuters on Monday evening.

Earlier truces have held a day or so but have disintegrated into fresh mortar and rocket exchanges which have put tens of thousands of civilians to flight and devastated the capital of the oil-producing former French colony.

U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who helped negotiate the truce proposed by Bongo, said on Sunday the talks would focus on national reconciliation and creating an environment for a presidential election in the next two months.
The bloody showdown began on June 5 when soldiers surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militias ahead of a now-postponed July 27 presidential election.
Lissouba, Sassou and Brazzaville mayor and national mediator Bernard Kolelas, whose militia has kept out of the latest fighting, planned to contest the July 27 election.

The sound of mortar and heavy machinegun fire was heard across the river in the Democratic Republic of the Congo capital Kinshasa around nightfall on Monday and between 10 p.m. and 10.30 p.m., witnesses said.
"There was some sporadic shooting during the day, but until the shelling started it had been relatively calm compared to recent days," said an aid worker returning from Brazzaville.
As part of mediation efforts, plans are taking shape for a U.N.-sponsored, mainly African peacekeeping force.
Lissouba's mandate expires at the end of August. He says the constitution allows a 90-day extension to organise elections. Sassou demands a national salvation government.
Kolelas's militia was at the heart of similar political and ethnic clashes that killed at least 2,000 people in Brazzaville after a disputed 1993 parliamentary election.
